blocks.text: Paul presents the death, burial, resurrection, and appearances of Christ as a tradition he received and passed on. The named appearances—to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles, and Paul—form the testimony from which the chapter’s discussion of future resurrection proceeds.

Paul argues that denying resurrection of the dead would also undermine the proclamation that Christ was raised, with consequences for faith, witness, forgiveness, those who have died, and hope. Verse 29’s reference to people “baptized for the dead” remains underdetermined: it does not identify the people, the dead, the ritual’s logic, or Paul’s endorsement. The verse therefore supports Paul’s local argument about resurrection, not certainty about a universal proxy rite or postmortem benefit. His references to continual danger make the same argumentative point and should not be turned into pressure toward unsafe exposure, martyrdom, or rejection of rescue and care.

In response to “How are the dead raised?” Paul uses the image of sowing: a seed dies, yet God gives it a body, and each seed retains its particularity. The analogy explains continuity through transformation, not the biological mechanics of resurrection. It does not establish rules about burial, cremation, or bodily donation.

The cry over death in verses 54–55 reuses Hosea within Paul’s resurrection argument. That later use should be read as such; it does not erase the threat-filled literary setting of the Hosea passage itself.

“Firstfruits” marks Christ as first in the order Paul states: those who belong to him follow at his arrival, and death is the last enemy to be abolished. Likewise, “flesh and blood cannot inherit” is immediately paired with perishability and with the promised transformation of both dead and living into imperishability and immortality. The phrase therefore does not treat matter, present bodily difference, or sex traits as intrinsically evil.

A “spiritual body” in this passage remains a body: Paul contrasts perishable, dishonored, weak existence with an embodied life raised imperishable, glorious, and powerful. This guards against reading “spiritual” as immaterial or as freedom from embodied identity. The chapter’s transformed-body language does not prescribe one normalized appearance or exclude disability, intersex traits, scars, aging, or medical alteration. Its victory over death also does not suppress grief, and its call to steadfast work does not make burnout, dangerous work, or trauma endurance a requirement.

The extant text of 1 Corinthians is best read as a coherent rhetorical whole, while proposals that particular passages are interpolations or that the letter is a compilation remain matters for passage-by-passage evaluation. Manuscript witnesses preserve portions and variants of the letter, but no single witness simply equals the original copy.
